title: India Is Now Under Fire From Both Sides in the Gulf. The U.S. Struck Its Sailors. Trump Says Iran Attacked Its Ships Too.
excerpt: Three Indian seafarers are dead from a U.S. Navy strike. Hours later, Trump accused Iran of launching drones at Indian vessels. Jaishankar called Rubio to protest. India's 300,000 merchant sailors are caught in the middle of a war they played no part in starting.
body:
## India Is Now Under Fire From Both Sides in the Gulf. The U.S. Struck Its Sailors. Trump Says Iran Attacked Its Ships Too.

In the space of 72 hours this week, India found itself in the worst possible position in the Strait of Hormuz crisis: caught in the crossfire between two belligerents, its sailors attacked by both, and its diplomatic options narrowing by the day.

On one side, the United States Navy struck three commercial tankers crewed by Indian seafarers off the coast of Oman between Monday and Thursday. Three Indian sailors aboard the Palau-flagged tanker MT Settebello were killed, while the status of the remaining crew members remains uncertain. Twenty-one others were rescued after jumping overboard. Another vessel, the MT Jalveer, was hit by two Hellfire missiles fired into its engine room. Its 20 Indian crew members survived.

On the other side, Donald Trump accused Iran of launching a drone attack against Indian ships leaving the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday night, calling it "totally unacceptable" in a Truth Social post. U.S. forces subsequently shot down multiple Iranian one-way attack drones heading toward the Strait, according to a source who spoke to Reuters.

"Their totally rebuffed Drone attack last night against Indian Ships leaving the Hormuz Strait is TOTALLY UNACCEPTABLE," Trump wrote. "They better get their act together, and FAST!"

Iran's Foreign Ministry responded by condemning the American strikes on Indian-crewed vessels, calling them "armed robbery and state piracy" and expressing condolences to the families of the dead sailors.

India, in other words, is being offered sympathy by both sides — and protection by neither. This precarious situation not only affects the families of the sailors but also has broader implications for the Indian diaspora, particularly those in the maritime industry. Many NRIs depend on remittances from seafarers, and disruptions in their safety can lead to financial instability for families back home.

## 'Such Lethal Actions Are Not Justified'

External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar spoke to U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday evening to deliver what the ministry called a "strong protest" — the most pointed diplomatic language New Delhi has used against Washington in years.

"Spoke to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio this evening. I reiterated India's strong protest at the attacks by the US Navy in the Gulf that killed three Indian mariners," Jaishankar wrote on X. "Such lethal actions against commercial shipping are not justified."

Hours earlier, the Ministry of External Affairs had summoned U.S. Chargé d'Affaires Jason Meeks for the second time in two days — a rare double summoning that underscored the severity of India's displeasure.

The U.S. State Department, for its part, responded with a message that stopped well short of an apology. Secretary Rubio "stressed that all commercial vessels should immediately comply with orders from U.S. forces," a department statement said, adding that violations of the blockade and "illicit transport of Iranian oil" would not be tolerated.

## The Human Cost

The diplomatic friction conceals a far more visceral crisis. India is the world's second-largest supplier of merchant marine labour, with over 300,000 seafarers working globally, according to the Forward Seamen's Union of India. Many of them serve on foreign-flagged vessels operating in the volatile Gulf, where they are the most exposed workers in a war between two governments that claim to be India's partners.

Sushila Devi, the wife of one of the dead sailors, Shivanand Chaurasia — the sole earner in a family with two young children from Deoria in northern India — collapsed in grief when informed of his death. "If he had told us about the dangers, I would have called him back," she said. "The government should not allow people to go there."

The Forward Seamen's Union's general secretary Manoj Yadav said the attacks had triggered "panic and fear" among Indian seafarers stranded in the Gulf since the conflict began in February. He questioned why U.S. forces fired missiles at a commercial vessel carrying no ammunition when they could have taken alternative measures to ensure safety.

As tensions escalate, the impact on the Indian diaspora is becoming increasingly pronounced. Many families are now grappling with the uncertainty of their loved ones' safety at sea, which could affect not only emotional ties but also financial stability through remittances. The Indian government faces mounting pressure to advocate for its citizens abroad and ensure their safety in these turbulent waters.
